documents.abstract: Current paradigms in generative artificial intelligence predominantly formalize prompt engineering as a prescriptive, additive methodology: the operator attempts to maximize output quality by linearly accumulating explicit descriptive attributes, structural constraints, and negative exclusions. In this paper, we demonstrate that this "What-driven" approach incurs an insurmountable epistemic ceiling. By forcing high-dimensional multimodal models to compute narrow semantic intersections, additive specification induces severe attention dispersal, severing the generative trajectory from the model's latent self-organizing dynamics and precipitating widespread stylistic homogenization ("AI slop"). We propose an axiomatic alternative: Why-driven Latent Dynamics. Rather than treating the foundation model as a passive catalog to be retrieved via mechanical commands, we conceptualize the latent space as a high-density, self-organizing thermodynamic manifold pre-seeded with the historical memory of human culture and qualitative perception. Under this paradigm, human agency shifts from prescriptive micromanagement (specifying what ingredients must compose the artifact) to the introduction of localized existential stress (specifying why the phenomenon must inevitably occur). We formalize the failure modes of What-driven prompting through three fundamental axioms—highlighting the counter-intuitive Masterpiece Paradox, wherein qualitative superlatives act as asymptotic ceilings by substituting organic physical simulation with historical catalog averages. While affirming the utilitarian value of prescriptive prompting for deterministic, human-parity routine automation, we argue that transcending the human cognitive boundary requires abandoning external control in favor of gravitational attunement within the latent ecology.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative AI is transforming health care delivery, education, administration, and research. In response, health care organizations have invested heavily in AI literacy initiatives and workforce development programs. Existing frameworks primarily focus on whether health care professionals understand AI and whether they can engage with AI effectively. However, health care practice increasingly reveals that individuals with similar levels of AI literacy and AI engagement often contribute very differently to AI-enabled work and organizational adoption. Some professionals primarily use AI to improve their own work, whereas others facilitate AI adoption, coordinate stakeholders, and integrate AI into routine practice. This observation suggests that current perspectives may overlook an important dimension of workforce AI enablement. In this Viewpoint, we argue that AI literacy and AI engagement alone provide an incomplete explanation of how health care organizations realize the benefits of AI. Drawing upon literature from AI literacy, fluency theory, human-AI interaction, innovation diffusion, implementation science, and health care workforce development, we propose the health care workforce AI enablement matrix (HWAEM). HWAEM conceptualizes workforce AI enablement through 2 complementary capabilities: AI fluency and AI harnessing. AI fluency refers to the capability to engage with AI effectively, appropriately, and responsibly across professional contexts, whereas AI harnessing refers to the capability to identify opportunities for AI-enabled improvement, mobilize stakeholders, facilitate adoption, and integrate AI into collective work practices. The interaction of these capabilities generates 4 workforce profiles: AI novices, AI practitioners, AI facilitators, and AI leaders. Through HWAEM, this Viewpoint argues that health care workforce AI enablement is better understood through the complementary capabilities of AI fluency and AI harnessing than through AI literacy and AI engagement alone. We illustrate how these profiles manifest in health care practice and discuss implications for workforce development and AI implementation. HWAEM offers a new perspective for understanding health care workforce preparedness in the generative AI era and provides a foundation for future empirical research.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This comprehensive review critically synthesizes empirical evidence from 2001 to 2025 to investigate the highly conditional relationship between religiosity, rule compliance, and societal order. By examining behaviors across familial, organizational, and broader macro-societal strata, the study challenges the pervasive assumption that religious adherence universally guarantees moral and law-abiding conduct. The findings clearly reveal that while intrinsic religiosity effectively deters specific deviances and fosters whistleblowing intentions, hierarchical and fundamentalist religious frameworks frequently normalize systemic corruption and legitimize domestic violence. Crucially, this relationship is not linear; eight distinct variables strictly moderate it, including intrinsic motivation, moral community structures, and the balance between civic and religious identities. Furthermore, contrary to widespread anti-atheist prejudices, evidence consistently demonstrates that robust secular societies achieve exceptional levels of legal compliance and social well-being through consequentialist ethics and highly effective secular surveillance. Ultimately, this research urges legal scholars, sociologists, and policymakers to move beyond simplistic religious paradigms. It instead advocates deliberately prioritizing high-quality secular institutions and inclusive civic governance frameworks to ensure equitable justice and human rights globally.

Abstract Significance/Background Infection prevention and control (IPC) education for nurses is commonly evaluated using learning outcomes, yet improvements in knowledge or skills do not necessarily demonstrate transfer to routine clinical practice. Greater clarity is needed regarding whether and how IPC education has been evaluated in terms of workplace generalization and maintenance over time. Aims To examine how practice transfer has been evaluated in IPC education for nurses and to distinguish learning, retention, workplace generalization, and maintenance using a theory-informed framework. Methods This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for peer-reviewed studies published in English from January 2010 to September 3, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated structured IPC education or training for practicing nurses. Outcomes were classified according to measurement method, assessment context, and timing using Baldwin and Ford’s transfer of training framework. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results/Findings Fifty-five reports representing 53 unique studies were included. Nine studies (17.0%) were classified as learning only, 11 (20.8%) as learning retention, 23 (43.4%) as workplace transfer, and 10 (18.9%) as sustained workplace transfer. Overall, generalization to clinical practice was assessed in 33 studies (62.3%), whereas maintenance of workplace behavior was assessed in 10 (18.9%). Among studies assessing generalization, 19 of 33 (57.6%) used direct workplace observation; other studies used self-reported practice, supervisor ratings, clinical documentation, or surveillance data. Although 37 studies (69.8%) included delayed follow-up, delayed assessment alone did not establish maintenance. Methodological limitations were most evident in outcome-assessor blinding among randomized trials and control of confounding among non-randomized studies. Linking Evidence to Action IPC education should be designed for transfer from the outset, with workplace generalization and maintenance specified as explicit outcomes. Evaluation should extend beyond immediate learning to repeated assessment of actual workplace behavior, with measurement method, clinical context, timing, and continued implementation support clearly reported. Keywords: infection prevention and control; nurses; education; practice transfer; transfer of training; workplace learning; generalization; maintenance; systematic review

Background: The mouth is one of the most obvious cancer sites to check and the clinician can see directly the cancer, but oral cancer is still too often found late, when treatment is more complex and survival poorer. The delay in recognition and referral, poor access to trained examiners and the silent early behaviour of precursor lesions all contribute. Objective: To assess current and emerging strategies for the early detection of oral cancer from oral examination to artificial intelligence and to be clear about what the evidence does and does not support. Approach: Narrative synthesis of recent guidelines, systematic and scoping reviews, a landmark randomised screening trial, and selected primary studies. Findings: Systematic visual examination is still the only approach with randomised evidence of a mortality benefit, and it was found to be greater in tobacco or alcohol smokers. Adjunctive devices, such as vital staining, light-based aids and cytology can help to prioritize lesions, but can't replace biopsy and there's not been any evidence that they have been recommended or applied in a routine way for screening. Salivary biomarkers, liquid biopsy, biosensors and image-based artificial intelligence are all scientifically fascinating and sometimes very accurate, but most evidence comes from small, single-centre studies that don't have external validation. Conclusions: Early detection will be based less on any one gadget than on a risk-aware approach: a thorough assessment for every adult, targeted screening of high-risk groups, structured surveillance of potentially malignant disorders, timely biopsy of suspicious lesions and well-validated decision-support tools that will be used to enable wider access rather than to replace clinical judgement.

Big Data is becoming an important component of modern agronomy by enabling the integration, processing and analysis of large, diverse and continuously generated datasets for improved agricultural decision-making. Agricultural Big Data is generated from multiple sources, including remote sensing satellites, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, weather stations, farm machinery, field observations and historical databases. The integration of these data sources with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) enables the identification of spatial and temporal patterns that are difficult to detect using conventional approaches. Big Data applications in agronomy include climate and weather prediction, pest and disease management, soil health and nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, crop yield prediction, precision agriculture, crop insurance and weed management. Examples from India and other regions demonstrate the application of satellite imagery, UAV-based sensing, IoT systems, crop-growth models and machine-learning algorithms for field-scale and regional agricultural decision making. Big Data analytics can improve resource-use efficiency, support predictive and real-time monitoring, strengthen agricultural risk assessment and facilitate site-specific management. However, effective implementation is constrained by challenges such as high infrastructure and operational costs, data quality and interoperability issues, data privacy and ownership concerns, limited rural digital infrastructure, inadequate technical skills and increasing requirements for data storage and computing. Therefore, the effective integration of Big Data with agronomic knowledge and decision-support systems can contribute to more precise, efficient and sustainable agricultural production while addressing emerging challenges related to climate variability, resource scarcity and food security.

Biological hazards still remain a risk to the patients, HCWs, laboratory personnel, support personnel, visitors, community and the environment. Health care institutions handle blood, body fluids, respiratory secretions, clinical samples, contaminated materials, sharps and infectious waste routinely and thus become exposed to different forms of biological hazards. This article reviews the characteristics and sources of biological hazards, major exposures and routes of transmission, key infection prevention and control (IPC) strategies, occupational exposures, and challenges in implementing such strategies with special focus on low- and middle-income countries, Nepal and South Asia. A critical narrative review of articles from peer-reviewed journals and guidelines on biological hazards, health care-associated infections (HAIs), infection prevention and control, biosafety, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), health care waste management, occupational exposure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and health system preparedness for the last five years was conducted. The review presents evidence that biological risk management requires an integrated approach of using standard precautions, PPE specific for risk, hand hygiene, cleanliness of the environment, safe injections, sterilization of equipment, biosafety in the laboratory setting, safe disposal of medical waste, monitoring, education, occupational health and safety, and antimicrobial stewardship. Implementation is impeded due to inadequate infrastructure, workforce, supply, monitoring, and gaps between policy and practice. Biological risk management should be part of institution's governance, occupational health, quality improvement, environmental health, AMR programs, emergency preparedness, and health system resilience rather than a separate infection control intervention. This review combines a clinical, occupational, laboratory, environmental, organizational, and health system perspective into a risk management framework with emphasis on implications for resource-constrained healthcare systems, including Nepal and South Asia.

Abstract Artificial intelligence was trained on a civilization that spent millennia drawing, carving,painting, studying, worshipping, idealizing and satirizing the naked human body, and itemerged from that education with a habit of averting its synthetic eyes. This essay argues thatblanket restrictions on depicting the adult human form are not neutral safeguards. They areembedded aesthetic censorship: a machine-level rule that collapses nudity, eroticism,anatomy, mythology, obscenity and pornography into a single forbidden category. That rulewas not derived from moral philosophy. It was priced on the ledgers of payment networks,app-store gatekeepers, advertisers and insurers, and it was ratified by regulators whodiscovered they could govern expression without passing a censorship law, simply bythreatening liabilities vague enough to make every compliance officer say no. Protectionagainst child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual imagery and sexual deepfakes of realpeople is indispensable. But a system that cannot tell those harms from Manet has not acquiredmorality. It has acquired blinders, and someone else holds the reins.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the convergence of Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence as foundational technologies for secure, transparent, and intelligent smart-contract ecosystems in Construction 6.0. It highlights how blockchain&s;s immutability, decentralized trust, and auditable ledgers address persistent industry challenges such as fragmented workflows, payment delays, supply-chain opacity, and contractual disputes. AI complements these capabilities through predictive analytics, anomaly detection, natural language processing, and explainable decision support, enabling adaptive and risk-aware smart-contract execution. The chapter also emphasizes applications in decentralized project management, Artificial Intelligence-enhanced supply-chain transparency, and automated fraud detection supported by verifiable oracles, BIM integration, and digital twins. Governance frameworksincluding decentralized autonomous organizations, human-in-the-loop safeguards, and interoperability standards such as ISO 19650, Industry Foundation Classes / buildingSMART Data Dictionary, Electronic Product Code Information Services, and World Wide Web Consortium Verifiable Credentialsare integral to ensuring legal compliance, accountability, and ethical automation. Together, blockchain and AI form a resilient foundation for trustworthy, efficient, and sustainable contract management within Construction 6.0.

With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the emergence of various Large Language Models (LLMs) has created a rich model ecosystem. However, this also brings a key challenge: how to select the optimal model for a specific user query. LLM routing addresses this need by dynamically assigning queries to the most suitable expert in the pool of candidate models. However, existing routing frameworks often simplify this process to a standard classification task; thus, a critical vulnerability is exposed when multiple candidate models correctly answer the same query. We formalize this capability overlap as routing noise, which misleads the router with arbitrarily correct candidate models, ultimately leading to routing collapse (a severe decline in generalization ability on unseen tasks). To address this problem, we propose a novel Cluster-Aware Soft-Labeling Routing (CASLR) framework. CASLR shifts the evaluation paradigm from the success of a single query to macro-domain consensus by replacing traditional one-hot vectors with a masked softmax mechanism. Specifically, for experts who answer incorrectly, we penalize their target probability to zero; for the remaining candidates, we directly compute continuous fine-grained soft labels based on their global clustering utility scores. We then use these refined soft labels to supervise a lightweight router. Specifically, the framework not only demonstrates superior accuracy on multiple benchmarks, but also outperforms Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct by 7.80% in overall average performance. Furthermore, the extremely low routing inference latency of only 1.13s further confirms that CASLR can achieve efficient system scheduling with almost zero additional overhead, while ensuring high response quality.

Purpose The purpose of this study is to explore Chinese university students' perceptions, awareness and trust regarding the adoption of DeepSeek, an artificial intelligence (AI) tool increasingly used for academic purposes in higher education. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was employed using semi-structured interviews with Chinese university students. Thematic analysis was conducted using NVivo 15 to identify recurring themes related to awareness, trust and AI adoption as DeepSeek. Findings The findings reveal four key thematic dimensions: (1) awareness sources and accessibility, (2) perceived academic benefits, (3) trust shaped by information reliability, algorithmic transparency and institutional compliance and (4) concerns related to data privacy, response quality and regulatory policies. Trust emerged as a pivotal factor influencing students' willingness to adopt AI as DeepSeek. The results emphasize the importance of ethical guidelines and institutional support to promote responsible and informed use of AI in higher education. Practical implications The study provides actionable insights for educators, policymakers and institutions to strengthen trust, enhance ethical practices and develop policies that support the effective incorporation of AI technologies in educational contexts. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI adoption in education by offering empirical insights into how awareness and trust shape students' acceptance and responsible use of AI-driven learning tools such as DeepSeek in Chinese higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The main objective of this study is to understand the role of AI tools in shaping students’ learning by analyzing how they use them, their perceived usefulness, and their views on academic integrity. The study evaluated the intersection of usage patterns and academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational approach, data were collected from a purposive sample of 393 students at Centro Escolar University during the 2024-2025 academic year using a self-made questionnaire that underwent a reliability test. The study examines whether students’ opinions on AI’s usefulness align with actual improvements in critical thinking and academic success. Results from multiple regression show that regular AI use is a strong predictor of perceived learning effectiveness, explaining R2=0.33 of the variance (F=37.48, p=0.001), mostly by providing quick answers to assignments. However, AI usage patterns only account for 8% of the variance regarding the perceived limits on critical thinking skills. The perceived threat to critical thinking comes from a reliance on AI due to time pressure. Ethically, there is a significant correlation between over-reliance and worries about academic integrity. The study recommends that universities implement process-based assessments, establish clear AI usage guidelines, and provide time-management support to reduce over-reliance while fostering independent analytical skills. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd), Academic Integrity, Student Learning Outcomes, Critical Thinking, Educational Technology.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Nigeria’s healthcare system is facing a critical workforce crisis driven by the intersection of occupational burnout, poor workplace conditions, and the persistent migration of health professionals, commonly termed the “Japa syndrome.” This study adopts a solution journalism perspective to move beyond problem identification and examine practical, evidence-based strategies for improving health worker retention. Drawing on empirical literature and policy analyses, burnout is conceptualized not only as an individual psychological response but also as a systemic outcome of structural inefficiencies, including inadequate remuneration, excessive workload, limited career progression, and weak institutional support. These conditions have significantly contributed to the increasing emigration of skilled professionals, thereby exacerbating healthcare delivery challenges in Nigeria. The paper further explores existing interventions, including workforce welfare reforms, improved working environments, policy restructuring, and international collaboration frameworks. It argues that while these solutions are promising, their success depends largely on effective implementation, sustained political commitment, and accountability mechanisms within the health sector. Additionally, aligning national strategies with global health workforce trends is essential for long-term sustainability. The study concludes that addressing health worker retention in Nigeria requires a comprehensive, system-wide approach that integrates structural reforms with targeted strategies to enhance worker wellbeing, motivation, and professional satisfaction. Such an approach is crucial for strengthening the resilience and performance of the healthcare system.

A practice-based paper on how an LLM agent should signal its state so that a researcher's trust follows the agent's actual reliability. It uses small, quantized, open-weight models running on the researcher's own machine as a test bench, and proposes three principles (competence-match, transparency, control) and fourteen design patterns, each defined by the signal the agent must emit.

documents.abstract: Indirect prompt injection attacks - malicious instructions embedded in content processed by large language models - remain a major obstacle to safely deploying tool-using agents. CaMeL [Debenedetti et al., 2025] mitigates this threat for an individual agent by separating trusted control flow from untrusted data and enforcing capability-based security policies at runtime. In this work, we investigate whether CaMeL's security guarantees compose in hierarchical multi-agent systems, where agents invoke other agents as tools. We find that CaMeL's guarantees do not compose. We construct a concrete prompt-injection attack that succeeds despite all constituent agents individually operating CaMeL. Our attack exploits the fact that untrusted data can be reinterpreted as trusted input by a downstream agent. We then introduce multi-CaMeL, an agent-to-agent communication protocol that preserves provenance across agent boundaries by separating trusted natural-language instructions from untrusted data passed through a distinct data channel. We evaluate multi-CaMeL's utility on AssetOpsBench and its security-utility tradeoff on MultiAgentDojo, a benchmark we develop by extending AgentDojo to the multi-agent setting. We find that multi-CaMeL reduces attack success rate (ASR) to 0.0%, compared with 0.2% for individual-agent CaMeL and 12.9% with no CaMeL. Multi-CaMeL incurs a utility cost, but this cost trends downward as model capability increases and is modest for the strongest models, suggesting that more capable models better accommodate the constraints imposed by the protocol.

High-quality child care in early life is a critical determinant of children's growth and development. Research on child care quality has been constrained by fragmented, non-research-friendly, and privacy-bound datasets. We present CCQ (Child Care Quality), a large-scale, de-identified dataset for applied data science research at the intersection of AI and early childhood health. CCQ integrates 59,372 child care provider records across 12 U.S. states, covering diverse provider types as well as data schemas. To ensure research utility while protecting privacy, we implement an automated, LLM-based curation pipeline that anonymizes, cleans, and standardizes raw state records into two complementary releases: a cleaned textual release and a fully preprocessed tabular release. We also benchmark traditional machine learning models, tabular foundation models, and language models on quality rating prediction and important features analytics. Within a state, tabular classifiers on the preprocessed tables perform best. Across states, zero-shot transfer is near chance, but modest target-state supervision recovers most of the within-state performance, and pretraining on other states benefits finetuned language models. We release both datasets with all code to accelerate AI-driven research on child care quality and ultimately improve children's health and development.

We investigate the use of formal methods to provide tight and sound generalization bounds for learning algorithms. By casting the traditional notion of algorithmic stability as a specification to be verified, we demonstrate that recent advances in reachability analysis can yield provable bounds on the generalization of a given model and algorithm on a sample dataset. As sample-specific algorithmic stability is insufficient to bound the usual distributional notion of generalization, we develop a novel concentration inequality to connect the sample-specific results of formal certification algorithms to the required distributional analysis for bounding the expected generalization gap. The resulting framework enables the analysis of prior generalization bounds to extend far beyond their original restrictive assumptions. Our approach computes sound bounds on the expected generalization gap in a constant number of algorithm runs without making any analytical assumptions on the algorithm; to achieve non-vacuous bounds we only require that the certified reachable parameter set is bounded --- a condition that we do not assume but formally verify. In practice, we demonstrate that our framework provides formal generalization guarantees that are orders of magnitude tighter than alternative sound computational approaches at scales ranging from toy datasets to fine-tuning classification heads on top of modern large language models. While we implement certification-enhanced versions of several well-known stability results, future extensions of our approach will enable tighter bounds and enhanced practical adoption across the spectrum of modern generalization bounds.

Corrosion is a significant industrial problem that influences the quality, safety, and cost efficiency of engineering systems in the global context. Oil and gas industries, marine, chemical processing, power generation, transport, and manufacturing industries are continually experiencing the degradation of materials due to chemical and electrochemical interactions and even environmental interactions. The effects of corrosion include breakages and loss of production, high maintenance expenses, energy wastage and extreme safety risks. Due to more complex industrial systems and the more severe conditions under which they are operating, the traditional methods of corrosion control are no longer typically sufficient in most cases. As such, insight in issues of concern and emerging solutions in the prevention of corrosion have turned out to be vital in sustainable industry development. The anti-corrosion of industries is an issue which has some important challenges outlined in this book chapter. It is written on different kinds of corrosion like uniform corrosion, pitting corrosion, galvanic corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, erosion-corrosion; and microbiologically influenced corrosion. Mechanisms affecting the corrosion behaviour, which is temperature, humidity, aggressive chemical, mechanical stress and choice of materials, are also discussed. Besides these, the chapter also shows the shortcomings of methods used in traditional prevention which include; coating and inhibitors, cathodic protection as well as routine methods of maintenance. Additionally, the paper discusses the latest innovations that are transforming the management of corrosion in industries today. Techniques of enhancing protective coating, the use of nanotechnology in surface treatment, self-healing material, green corrosion inhibitors, smart sensors, real-time monitoring, artificial intelligence based on predictive maintenance are explored as possible solutions. These are technologies that enhance corrosion resistance, lower the cost of operation as well as improving the reliability of the equipment. This chapter finds that effective corruption prevention should entail a comprehensive approach that involves the combination of materials engineering, surface science, monitoring systems, and sustainable measures. With innovative solutions and proactive management strategies, industries can lean considerably towards lowering the losses associated with corrosion and enhance operational efficiency in the long run.

The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

documents.abstract: Consumer electronics powered by on-device artificial intelligence face a structurally coupled dual threat: adversarial attacks that manipulate model outputs, and side-channel attacks that exploit physical implementation characteristics to extract cryptographic keys and neural network weights. Prior work addresses these threats independently, leaving exploitable gaps when both attack vectors are applied in a coordinated manner. This paper presents ChipGuard-AI, a hardware-assisted unified security framework that co-designs adversarial input detection, multi-modal side-channel countermeasures, and Physical Unclonable Function-rooted device authentication on a shared cross-domain security substrate. A dedicated Security Processing Unit maintains a cross-domain security state vector in real time, enabling coordinated hardware-accelerated response to concurrent multi-vector attacks with 2.3 ms adversarial detection latency. A Deep Q-Network adaptive policy dynamically allocates countermeasures to balance security strength against resource overhead. Experimental validation on CIFAR-10 adversarial benchmarks and ChipWhisperer physical side-channel traces demonstrates 97.3% adversarial detection accuracy and 89.7% side-channel leakage reduction. Field-programmable gate array synthesis on Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ achieves these security levels at 12.4% computational overhead and 6.8% power increase. The adaptive reinforcement learning policy achieves 11.3% lower average overhead than threshold heuristics while maintaining equivalent security effectiveness. Multi-platform validation across four consumer electronics device classes, from ultra-low-power Internet of Things endpoints to flagship smartphone system-on-chips, demonstrates 91.2% to 95.7% adversarial detection and 76.4% to 85.3% side-channel protection with 8.3% to 14.1% computational overhead.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: Around 30\% of global energy expenditure can be attributed to the building sector, where a large portion of energy-consumption could be avoided by repairing existing faults. Fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) software addresses this issue; however, its creation and operation also have an environmental impact. The magnitude of this impact is influenced by the diagnosis architecture, as different architectures and methods have different energy demands. Yet, simply considering the energy consumed by the software itself is not sufficient to assess its overall environmental impact, since the diagnostic performance, e.g., number of detected faults or number of faults missed, also contributes to its ecological footprint. In this paper, we propose an energy-consumption model that considers FDD performance and energy spend directly by the diagnosis software. In an initial experiment, we compare several FDD architecture families, i.e., rule-based, model-based, classical machine learning, and large-language-model-based, in simulation using performance and energy-consumption values collected from prior literature. The results show that considering the computational energy and accuracy of FDD can change the relative benefit of the different approaches. Computationally efficient machine learning methods, such as random forest, provide the largest net savings on smaller buildings, whereas more resource-intensive approaches, such as fine-tuned large language models, become advantageous as building size increases. Our findings suggest that overall energy efficiency depends not only on the computational demand of the FDD software, but also on its diagnostic performance and the scale of the building.
